\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Walsh noise operator]
\lean{FABL.noiseOperator}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p055-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p034-b004}
\label{FABL.noiseOperator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.monomial, FABL.walshBasis}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\rho\in\mathbb R$. The noise operator on
real-valued functions on $\{\pm1\}^n$ is the linear operator that multiplies each Walsh
monomial indexed by a subset $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $\rho^{|S|}$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{3}
For every nonnegative integer $n$, real $\rho$, and subset $S\subseteq[n]$, the noise
operator on the $n$-dimensional sign cube sends the monomial $x\mapsto\prod_{i\in S}x_i$
to $\rho^{|S|}$ times that monomial.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
For every nonnegative integer $n$, real $\rho$, subset $S\subseteq[n]$, and
$x\in\{−1,1\}^n$, applying the noise operator with parameter $\rho$ to the monomial
indexed by $S$ and evaluating at $x$ gives $\rho^{|S|}\prod_{i\in S}x_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Kernel noise operator]
\lean{FABL.kernelNoiseOperator}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p055-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006
}
\label{FABL.kernelNoiseOperator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For a real parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the kernel noise operator sends a real-valued
function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube to the function whose value at $x$ is
the expectation of $f$ under the noise kernel at $x$. This defines a linear map over
$\mathbb{R}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel and spectral noise operators]
\lean{FABL.kernelNoiseOperator_eq_noiseOperator}
\label{FABL.kernelNoiseOperator_eq_noiseOperator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.kernelNoiseOperator, FABL.monomial, FABL.noiseOperator, FABL.noiseOperator_monomial_apply, FABL.parity_orthonormal_basis, FABL.pmfExpectation_noiseKernel_monomial, FABL.walshBasis}
\difficulty{3}
For every integer $n\ge 0$, every correlation parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and every
real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, the operator that averages the
function against the independent coordinate noise kernel with keep probability
$(1+\rho)/2$ equals the linear operator that multiplies each Walsh monomial of degree
$|S|$ by $\rho^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p034-b004}
\label{FABL.noiseOperator_apply_eq_pmfExpectation}
\leanok

\begin{definition}[Noise stability]
\lean{FABL.noiseStability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b001
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.noiseStability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube,
its noise stability at correlation $\rho$ is the expectation of $f(x)f(y)$ when $(x,y)$
is drawn from the correlated pair distribution with parameter $\rho$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Correlated disagreement probability]
\lean{FABL.correlatedDisagreementProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b004
}
\label{FABL.correlatedDisagreementProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and a Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube, the
correlated disagreement probability is the expectation, under the correlated pair
distribution with parameter $\rho$, of the indicator that $f(x)\ne f(y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Majority disagreement under correlated noise]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_correlatedDisagreementProbability_majority_odd}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b004
}
\label{FABL.tendsto_correlatedDisagreementProbability_majority_odd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.CorrelationPlane, FABL.coe_normalizedCorrelatedSignSumMeasure_disagreement_eq_majority, FABL.correlatedDisagreementProbability, FABL.correlatedGaussianMeasure, FABL.correlatedGaussianMeasure_disagreement, FABL.gaussianDisagreementRegion, FABL.majority, FABL.normalizedCorrelatedSignSumMeasure, FABL.normalizedCorrelatedSignSumMeasure_disagreement_tendsto}
\difficulty{4}
For every correlation parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the probability that majority on $2k+1$
independent uniform signs changes under coordinatewise noise with correlation $\rho$
converges, as $k\to\infty$, to $\arccos(\rho)/\pi$.
\end{theorem}

\label{FABL.two_div_pi_mul_arcsin_eq_one_sub_two_div_pi_mul_arccos}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\rho$, $\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho)=1-\frac{2}{\pi}\arccos(\rho)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Correlated agreement probability]
\lean{FABL.correlatedAgreementProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b001}
\label{FABL.correlatedAgreementProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and a Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube, the
correlated agreement probability is the expectation, under the correlated pair
distribution with parameter $\rho$, of the indicator that $f(x)=f(y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A centered interval bound]
\lean{FABL.one_sub_two_mul_mem_Icc}
\label{FABL.one_sub_two_mul_mem_Icc}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $\delta$ with $0\leq\delta\leq1$, the number $1-2\delta$ lies in
$[-1,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Noise sensitivity]
\lean{FABL.noiseSensitivity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p130-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p130-b005
}
\label{FABL.noiseSensitivity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.one_sub_two_mul_mem_Icc, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For $\delta\in[0,1]$ and a Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube, its
noise sensitivity at rate $\delta$ is the probability that $f(x)\ne f(y)$ when $(x,y)$
is drawn from the correlated pair distribution with parameter $1-2\delta$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $ho\in[-1,1]$, and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb
R$. Choose $X$ uniformly from the sign cube and, independently in each coordinate,
obtain $Y$ by keeping $X_i$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and otherwise flipping its
sign. If $T_\rho$ is the linear operator that multiplies each Walsh monomial of degree
$k$ by $\rho^k$, then $\mathbb E[f(X)f(Y)]=\langle f,T_\rho f\rangle$, where the inner
product is the uniform average over the sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a difference]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_sub}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_sub}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. The expectation of their pointwise difference is the
difference of their expectations: $\mathbb{E}_p[f-g]=\mathbb{E}_p[f]-\mathbb{E}_p[g]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation and scalar division]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_div}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_div}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, let
$f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. The expectation of the function
$x\mapsto f(x)/c$ under $p$ equals the expectation of $f$ divided by $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sign disagreement indicator]
\lean{FABL.boolean_disagreement_indicator}
\label{FABL.boolean_disagreement_indicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ map the discrete cube $\{-1,1\}^n$ to $\{-1,1\}$, and let $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$.
The indicator that $f(x)$ and $f(y)$ differ equals $\bigl(1-f(x)f(y)\bigr)/2$, viewing
the signs as real numbers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise sensitivity and noise stability]
\lean{FABL.noiseSensitivity_eq_half_sub_half_noiseStability}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b002}

  {context}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b003}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $0\le\delta\le1$, and let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional
sign cube to signs. Its noise sensitivity at rate $\delta$ equals one half of one minus
the noise stability of its real-valued version at correlation $1-2\delta$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b005}
\difficulty{3}
Let $-1\le\rho\le1$ and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$. For a correlated pair $(X,Y)$
formed by choosing $X$ uniformly from the sign cube and, independently in each
coordinate, keeping $X_i$ as $Y_i$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and otherwise flipping
its sign, the probability that $f(X)\ne f(Y)$ is $\bigl(1-\mathbb{E}[f(X)f(Y)]\bigr)/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise stability of odd-dimensional majority]
\lean{FABL.tendsto_noiseStability_majority_odd_arccos}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b002
}
\label{FABL.tendsto_noiseStability_majority_odd_arccos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.majority, FABL.noiseStability, FABL.tendsto_noiseStability_majority_odd, FABL.two_div_pi_mul_arcsin_eq_one_sub_two_div_pi_mul_arccos}
\difficulty{3}
For any correlation parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the noise stability of majority on $2k+1$
sign coordinates, evaluated on two uniformly distributed sign vectors coupled with
coordinate correlation $\rho$, tends as $k\to\infty$ to $1-(2/\pi)\arccos(\rho)$.
\end{theorem}

    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b002}
\difficulty{1}
For any $\delta\in[0,1]$, the noise sensitivity of majority on $2k+1$ sign coordinates,
with each coordinate independently flipped with probability $\delta$, tends as
$k\to\infty$ to $\arccos(1-2\delta)/\pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arccosine and arcsine identity]
\lean{FABL.arccos_one_sub_two_mul_eq_two_mul_arcsin_sqrt}
\label{FABL.arccos_one_sub_two_mul_eq_two_mul_arcsin_sqrt}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every $\delta\in[0,1]$, $\arccos(1-2\delta)=2\arcsin(\sqrt{\delta})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arcsine of one half]
\lean{FABL.arcsin_one_half}
\label{FABL.arcsin_one_half}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
The principal inverse sine of $1/2$ is $\pi/6$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arcsine difference bounds]
\lean{FABL.arcsin_sub_self_mem_Icc_two_mul_cube}
\label{FABL.arcsin_sub_self_mem_Icc_two_mul_cube}
\leanok
\difficulty{5}
For every $x\in[0,1/2]$, the difference $\arcsin(x)-x$ lies in $[0,2x^3]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cube of a Square Root]
\lean{FABL.sqrt_cube_eq_rpow_three_halves}
\label{FABL.sqrt_cube_eq_rpow_three_halves}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $x\ge 0$, $(\sqrt{x})^3=x^{3/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement and disagreement probabilities]
\lean{FABL.correlatedAgreementProbability_eq_one_sub_disagreement}
\label{FABL.correlatedAgreementProbability_eq_one_sub_disagreement}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.correlatedAgreementProbability, FABL.correlatedDisagreementProbability, FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one, FABL.pmfExpectation_sub}
\difficulty{4}
Let $-1\le\rho\le1$ and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$. For a correlated pair $(X,Y)$
formed by choosing $X$ uniformly from the sign cube and, independently in each
coordinate, keeping $X_i$ as $Y_i$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and otherwise flipping
its sign, the probability that $f(X)=f(Y)$ equals one minus the probability that
$f(X)\ne f(Y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise stability and agreement probability]

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b005}
\difficulty{3}
For every $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and every Boolean function $f$, its noise stability after
interpreting its outputs as real signs is twice the probability that its values agree on
a correlated pair of inputs, minus one.
\end{theorem}
